strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical question in multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection: whether task-specific training is necessary. The proposed RAD method is simple, easy to understand, and operationally appealing: frozen DINOv3 features, a memory bank, global retrieval, spatially constrained patch retrieval, and multi-layer score fusion.

The empirical evaluation is broad across MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM, with image-level and pixel-level metrics. The reported localization gains, especially in pixel AP/F1 on MVTec-AD and Real-IAD, are substantial.

The few-shot and cold-start analyses are useful and relevant. The results suggest that retrieval-based methods are particularly attractive when anomaly-free data are scarce or when new classes are introduced incrementally.
The ablation study supports the contribution of the main design components: multi-layer features, global context retrieval, and spatial conditioning each improve localization metrics.
The paper includes implementation details, per-category results, additional encoder/resolution analysis, and an explicit limitations section mentioning memory and latency costs.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not fully isolated from backbone and protocol advantages. RAD uses DINOv3 ViT-B/16 and 448-resolution inputs, while many baselines appear to be taken from prior work or use different encoders/training setups. The paper needs stronger fair-comparison baselines, especially memory/retrieval methods using the same DINOv3 backbone and resolution.

The novelty is somewhat overstated. RAD is essentially a nearest-neighbor memory method with global filtering, spatial constraints, and multi-layer features; this is a meaningful engineering combination, but it is close in spirit to PatchCore/SPADE/PaDiM and newer training-free or memory-based anomaly detectors. The claim of being the first training-free MUAD framework is insufficiently qualified.

The theoretical analysis is limited and partly overclaimed. Showing that distance-to-set is 1-Lipschitz and zero on stored normal embeddings does not by itself establish superior anomaly detection, AUROC, or robustness to anomalous-but-nearby feature embeddings. The “upper-bound” statement is mathematically narrow and does not justify the stronger claims made in the abstract and discussion.

The reconstruction-method critique relies on assumptions about bottlenecks, local benign variation subspaces, and decoder amplification that are plausible but not empirically validated on the compared models. The analysis does not demonstrate that the cited SOTA methods actually fail because of this fidelity-stability dilemma.

Several experimental choices are dataset-specific, including neighborhood radius and K values. It is unclear how these hyperparameters are selected without validation anomalies, and this weakens the training-free/reproducibility narrative.

Important efficiency data are missing. Since RAD stores dense multi-layer patch features and performs retrieval at inference time, memory footprint, indexing strategy, latency, and scaling behavior should be reported, especially on Real-IAD. The limitations mention cost but do not quantify it.

The standard MUAD table omits or underemphasizes direct comparisons to strong training-free memory baselines under the same unified multi-class setup. A DINOv3 PatchCore/SPADE-style baseline, naive all-memory retrieval, and same-backbone variants would be essential to attribute gains to RAD’s design rather than the encoder.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract says code is available but the link is blank, and single-seed reporting gives no sense of variability. The ethics/impact discussion is generic and does not engage with deployment risks such as false alarms/missed defects in safety-critical industrial settings.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical question: whether multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection really needs task-specific training. A simple training-free retrieval baseline is a useful direction, especially for cold-start and few-shot deployment settings.
The empirical results reported for RAD are strong on several standard benchmarks, particularly pixel-level AP/F1/AUPRO on MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and the RGB-only 3D-ADAM setting.

The method is conceptually simple: frozen ViT features, global image retrieval, spatially constrained patch retrieval, and multi-layer score fusion. This simplicity makes the approach potentially attractive if the claims are validated fairly.
The paper includes useful ablations for multi-layer memory, global context retrieval, and spatial conditioning, and reports per-class results in the appendix.
The limitations section acknowledges memory and inference-latency costs, which are real issues for retrieval-based anomaly detection.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not convincingly supported by fair comparisons. RAD uses a very strong and very recent DINOv3 ViT-B/16 encoder at 448 resolution, while many baselines are older trained methods with different backbones and resolutions. The paper does not provide controlled comparisons where leading baselines are upgraded to the same encoder/input regime, nor does it compare against a strong multi-class PatchCore/SPADE-style retrieval baseline using the same features.

Originality is overstated. Memory/retrieval-based anomaly detection with nearest-neighbor patch matching is a long-standing line of work, and the paper itself cites PaDiM, PatchCore, SPADE, PNI, memory-based MUAD, and UniVAD. The proposed combination of global retrieval, local spatial restriction, and multi-layer ViT features is plausible but appears incremental relative to this literature. Claims such as the first training-free MUAD framework to reach SOTA need much stronger positioning.

The theoretical contribution is weak and overclaimed. The distance-to-set score being 1-Lipschitz and zero on stored normal embeddings is elementary, and the propositions do not establish that retrieval generally upper-bounds reconstruction residuals in any useful anomaly-detection sense. In fact, the appendix shows Sret(zi) <= Srec(zi) only on stored normal embeddings, while the manuscript repeatedly describes retrieval as an upper bound on reconstruction-based scoring/performance. The analysis does not connect tightly to the actual cosine 1-NN, global top-K, spatial conditioning, multi-layer fusion, or benchmark outcomes.

The fidelity-stability dilemma analysis relies on assumptions that essentially encode the desired conclusion: if a bottleneck nearly preserves benign variations despite small singular values, the decoder must have large gain. This does not establish that practical reconstruction-based MUAD methods necessarily fail, nor does it explain why a memory method avoids all analogous instability from finite support, feature misalignment, or nearest-neighbor noise.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says the code is available but no URL is provided. Key implementation choices such as dataset-specific neighborhood radius and K values are given, but there is no validation protocol for selecting them. Retrieval memory size, feature dimensionality, exact preprocessing per dataset, runtime, and storage costs are not quantified despite being central limitations.

The evaluation emphasizes saturated image-level AUROC/AP metrics and does not sufficiently analyze statistically meaningful uncertainty, repeated runs, or sensitivity to hyperparameters. Since gains are often in dense localization metrics, small protocol differences in resizing, cropping, thresholding, and upsampling could materially affect conclusions.

The few-shot comparison is also not fully convincing: RAD benefits from a strong modern frozen backbone and retrieval design, while some baselines are vision-language or older methods with different capacities and protocols. The paper should include same-backbone nearest-neighbor and coreset baselines before concluding that RAD surpasses specialized few-shot methods.

Efficiency is underdeveloped. A method with K=900 retrieved images and multi-layer dense patch comparisons may be expensive on Real-IAD-scale memory banks, but the paper provides no wall-clock latency, memory footprint, approximate search setup, or scaling analysis. This weakens the practical significance claim.

The treatment of ethics/impact is perfunctory: the impact statement says no societal consequences need to be highlighted, which is inadequate for anomaly detection systems that may be deployed in safety-critical manufacturing, inspection, or quality-control settings.

Presentation is generally readable, but the paper repeatedly uses stronger language than the evidence supports, including 'overturns the assumption,' 'provably upper-bound,' and 'state-of-the-art' without sufficient controlled evidence. This makes the contribution feel less reliable than the reported numbers alone might suggest.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, compelling training-free retrieval framework for multi-class anomaly detection, combining global context retrieval, spatially conditioned patch matching, and multi-layer frozen features. The method is easy to understand and practically attractive for cold-start or class-incremental settings.

The empirical evaluation is broad and strong: results cover MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and a preliminary 3D-ADAM setting, with especially convincing gains in pixel-level localization metrics such as P-AP and P-F1. The few-shot and data-scaling experiments are useful and support the paper's central practical message.

The ablations are meaningful: multi-layer memory, global context retrieval, and spatial conditioning each contribute measurable gains, and the encoder/resolution study helps clarify when and why the method works.

The paper is generally well written and organized, with clear algorithmic motivation and useful appendices containing implementation details, per-category results, qualitative visualizations, and additional few-shot results.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are overstated. The retrieval score being zero on stored normal embeddings and 1-Lipschitz as a distance-to-set function is true but relatively elementary; it does not by itself establish that retrieval-based scoring generally upper-bounds or dominates reconstruction residuals for anomaly detection. The connection from these formal properties to the empirical superiority of RAD is suggestive rather than decisive.

The central question 'Is training necessary?' is not fully isolated experimentally. RAD relies heavily on a strong frozen DINOv3 encoder and large-scale external pretraining, while many baselines were not necessarily re-run with the same encoder, resolution, memory budget, or feature set. This makes it hard to attribute gains solely to avoiding task-specific training rather than to representation/backbone choices.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful implementation details. The abstract says code is available, but the manuscript appears to omit the actual URL. Hyperparameters are reported, but there is little detail on exact baseline reproduction, model selection, confidence intervals, memory footprint, retrieval implementation, or inference latency.

The limitations discussion is honest but too brief. Storage and retrieval latency are acknowledged, yet not quantified, even though they are central tradeoffs for a memory-based method. Failure modes beyond 3D background/viewpoint artifacts are not deeply analyzed.

The ethical and societal-impact discussion is generic and essentially states that no consequences need highlighting. For industrial anomaly detection, deployment issues such as false positives/false negatives, quality-control automation, and domain shift deserve at least a short substantive treatment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical question in multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection: whether task-specific training is necessary. The proposed RAD framework is simple, modular, and useful: global reference retrieval, spatially constrained patch matching, multi-layer features, and layer fusion are natural but effective design choices.

The empirical evaluation is broad and mostly convincing. RAD is tested on MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM, with standard MUAD, few-shot, cold-start scaling, encoder/resolution, ablation, hyperparameter sensitivity, unseen-normal, and memory-compression studies. The strongest evidence is the large localization gain over Dinomaly on MVTec-AD and Real-IAD, and the strong few-shot results with only 1-4 normal references.

The paper includes useful practical analysis. It reports memory footprint and latency, shows that global retrieval greatly reduces dense matching latency, and demonstrates that coreset compression can reduce MVTec-AD memory from 32.6 GB to 0.37 GB with limited degradation.

The method is likely reproducible in broad strokes: the appendix specifies backbone, feature layers, input resolution, neighborhood radii, top-K values, scoring rule, software stack, hardware, and seed. The ablations support the contribution of multi-layer memory, global retrieval, and spatial conditioning.
The writing is generally clear, and the paper gives a coherent motivation for replacing decoder reconstruction with retrieval in frozen feature space.
weaknesses: The central theoretical framing is somewhat overstated. The fidelity-stability dilemma for reconstruction methods is derived under stylized assumptions about bottlenecks, Jacobians, and local fidelity, but the paper does not directly validate the claimed amplification mechanism empirically across reconstruction baselines. The retrieval optimality result is also largely a property of distance-to-set scores within a restricted 1-Lipschitz class that vanishes on the memory, and does not by itself establish anomaly separability in realistic feature spaces.

Some SOTA claims are confounded by backbone and resolution choices. RAD uses DINOv3-B and 448-crop inputs, while many baselines in the main table appear to use their original settings. The same-backbone comparison with Dinomaly is helpful, but only covers one main competitor and does not fully isolate the contribution against other retrieval/few-shot methods or against upgraded versions of older baselines.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The method is a strong composition of known ideas from PatchCore/SPADE-style nearest-neighbor retrieval, global filtering, spatial conditioning, and multi-layer ViT features. The main novelty is adapting and validating this recipe for MUAD with strong modern encoders, not a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

The method has substantial resource requirements before compression: reported memory reaches 32.6 GB on MVTec-AD, 40.7 GB on VisA, and 60.8 GB on Real-IAD, and inference is slower than a pure feed-forward model. The coreset result is promising but only reported for MVTec-AD, so scalability on larger and more diverse datasets remains insufficiently established.

Reproducibility has gaps. The abstract says code is available but the URL is blank in the manuscript, and several details needed for exact replication/comparison are not fully clear, such as baseline reimplementation settings, whether all baselines use comparable preprocessing/resolution, and whether dataset-specific K and radius choices were tuned on validation/test performance.

The limitations and ethics discussion is too thin. The limitations mention storage and latency but not dependence on foundation encoder pretraining data, possible failure under unseen normal modes far from memory, dataset contamination risks, or deployment consequences of false negatives/false positives in industrial inspection. The impact statement says no societal consequences need highlighting, which is not very reflective for anomaly detection systems used in manufacturing or safety-relevant quality control.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reducing task-specific training for multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection, especially in few-shot and cold-start settings.

The proposed RAD pipeline is simple and practical: frozen ViT features, global context retrieval, spatially constrained patch matching, and multi-layer fusion. This simplicity is a strength if reproducible.
The empirical section is broad, covering MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM, with standard, few-shot, data-scaling, ablation, sensitivity, and memory-compression experiments.
The reported localization gains, especially in P-AP/P-F1 over Dinomaly on several benchmarks and in low-data settings, suggest that retrieval over strong frozen features is a useful direction.
The paper acknowledges important limitations around memory footprint and retrieval latency, and reports concrete memory numbers plus a coreset experiment on MVTec-AD.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially over-stated. The method is essentially a modernized nearest-neighbor feature-memory approach, closely related to PatchCore/SPADE/PNI-style retrieval methods, so the claim that it overturns the need for task-specific MUAD training is not convincingly established.

The theoretical contribution is weak. The fidelity-stability dilemma for reconstruction models relies on broad assumptions and does not show that practical reconstruction-based MUAD methods necessarily fail. The retrieval analysis is largely a property of distance-to-set functions under an artificially restricted 1-Lipschitz score class; it does not prove robustness in image space or superiority over learned methods.

The empirical evidence does not fully isolate method from backbone, resolution, and resource effects. RAD uses DINOv3-B and large memory banks, while many baselines appear to use their published configurations; the same-backbone comparison is relegated to a small appendix table and covers only Dinomaly on limited datasets/metrics.

The evaluation emphasizes saturated AUROC-style metrics and best-case localization improvements, but there is limited statistical analysis, no confidence intervals or multiple-run variance, and no clear accounting for validation choices or possible hyperparameter selection per dataset.

Reproducibility is not adequate for the strength of the claims. The abstract says code is available but the URL is blank in the provided manuscript; key implementation details such as preprocessing, image-level pooling, coreset construction, indexing/search implementation, thresholding, and random seeds are insufficiently specified.

The method has substantial deployment costs: reported memory footprints are 12.1/32.6/40.7/60.8 GB across datasets, and inference is much slower than a feed-forward model. The coreset result is promising but only shown on MVTec-AD, so scalability remains under-supported.

The impact/ethics statement is perfunctory, stating that no societal consequences need highlighting. For industrial anomaly detection, possible false negatives, false positives, deployment monitoring, and dataset/domain bias deserve at least minimal discussion.

Presentation is generally readable, but the tone is promotional. Phrases such as 'overturn the assumption' and 'first task-specific training-free MUAD framework' are not justified given prior retrieval-based anomaly detection literature.

strengths: The paper makes a clear and practically meaningful contribution: RAD shows that a simple training-free retrieval pipeline with global-context filtering, spatially constrained patch matching, and multi-layer feature fusion can outperform several trained MUAD systems. This is a useful reframing of the field, especially for cold-start and few-shot deployment settings where retraining is costly.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall. Results cover MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and an RGB-only 3D-ADAM setting, with image-level and pixel-level metrics. The gains are especially strong for localization, e.g. MVTec-AD P-AP improves from 69.3 for Dinomaly to 75.6 and Real-IAD P-AP from 42.8 to 53.7.

The few-shot and scaling experiments are a major strength. The paper evaluates single-class, multi-class, and incremental-class scaling and shows that RAD is sample-efficient and can incorporate new normal examples by updating memory rather than retraining.

The ablations are appropriate and support the main design choices. Multi-layer memory, global context retrieval, and spatial conditioning each improve localization, and the same-backbone comparison against Dinomaly with DINOv3 helps separate the retrieval contribution from backbone strength.

The paper is generally well organized and readable. The method is simple enough to reproduce conceptually, and the appendix gives useful implementation details, hyperparameter sweeps, per-category results, same-backbone comparisons, and memory-compression experiments.

The limitations around memory footprint and inference latency are treated honestly, and the coreset experiment is useful: on MVTec-AD, memory drops from 32.6 GB to 0.37 GB with relatively small degradation.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior memory/retrieval anomaly detectors such as SPADE, PatchCore, PaDiM/PNI-style position-aware methods, and recent training-free few-shot AD. The paper’s main advance is a strong MUAD instantiation and evaluation rather than a fundamentally new retrieval principle.

The theoretical analysis is correct but limited in force. The distance-to-set maximality and 1-Lipschitz properties follow from standard metric facts and do not by themselves establish that the frozen encoder space separates anomalies from unseen normal variations. The fidelity-stability dilemma for reconstruction methods is plausible, but the assumptions and conclusions are somewhat idealized.

The headline “task-specific training-free” claim should be interpreted carefully. RAD relies heavily on a very strong pretrained DINOv3 encoder, dataset-specific retrieval hyperparameters, high-resolution preprocessing, and large feature memories. This does not undermine the method, but it weakens the rhetorical claim that training is unnecessary in a broad sense.

Reproducibility is good in terms of algorithmic detail but still has gaps. The abstract says code is available but the URL is blank in the manuscript, and the experiments appear to use a single random seed. For a paper whose claims depend on strong empirical margins across protocols, public code and repeated-run variance would be important.

The efficiency story is mixed. Full-memory RAD requires 32.6 GB on MVTec-AD, 40.7 GB on VisA, and 60.8 GB on Real-IAD, with nontrivial inference latency. The coreset result is promising but only reported for MVTec-AD, so scalability to larger or less redundant datasets remains uncertain.

Some comparisons may still be affected by backbone and protocol differences. The same-backbone Dinomaly comparison is helpful, but most main-table baselines are not all upgraded to the same encoder/resolution/memory budget, making the absolute SOTA comparison less clean.

The impact statement is perfunctory. Industrial anomaly detection can affect safety-critical inspection, labor allocation, and false-negative/false-positive costs, so saying that no societal consequences need highlighting is weaker than expected for an ICML submission.
